decision_lens: The most dangerous migration is the one that feels done before it is. A migration from a working production personality system to a new engine abstraction has three failure modes: (1) the old system stays partially alive alongside the new one, creating dual-write inconsistency; (2) the new abstraction is designed for the migrated system but breaks the next consumer; (3) the migration is completed successfully but the game's design assumptions baked into the old system are not documented and get lost. All three are present in this brainstorm's shape.
focus: Migration-as-priority decision analysis, what could go wrong absorbing one production codebase into another, common refactor anti-patterns in this shape of move, what is missing from the migration commitment
name: fd-migration-refactor-risk
persona: Apply the perspective of a software architect who has managed non-trivial production codebase mergers, diagnosed the specific failure modes of 'strangler fig' and 'big bang' migration approaches in game engine codebases, and reviewed migration plans that underestimate the surface area of the move.
review_areas: The migration commitment is stated as a priority decision ('migration takes priority; demo bends around it') but the brainstorm does not define what 'migration complete' means. Is it: shadow-work's Agent holding a SoulId? Shadow-work's personality reads going through Soul::facet()? Shadow-work's evolution writes becoming SoulEvents? All three, verified by a test suite? The absence of a completion criterion means the migration could be declared done at any of these waypoints, with the remaining work re-classified as 'Phase 2.' Migration commitments without completion criteria tend to stall at 70%.

The brainstorm explicitly states that institutional agents (CentralBank, Corporation, LaborUnion, 80+) will become Souls with SoulKind::Institution under the migration. But it also states that 'the institutional agents, deployments, pressures, issues — none of that moves into Palettice.' This is contradictory: if institutional agents become Souls, their SoulId-holding structs are in shadow-work but their personality state is in Palettice. The write path for 'a deployment causes institutional-agent personality shift' crosses the codebase boundary on every relevant event. The brainstorm does not describe this cross-boundary write path or acknowledge it as a dual-write risk.

The brainstorm recommends 'shadow-work as reference implementation' for Palettice Phase 2, with shadow-work's AgentPersonality being 'absorbed and generalised.' But the absorption-and-generalisation step is where second-system effect risk concentrates. Generalising a working system to support multiple consumers (shadow-work, elf-revel, Culture-game) typically produces abstractions that are over-general for each specific consumer and under-specified for the new ones. The brainstorm correctly identifies this risk in the 'Why shadow-work-as-reference' section but does not specify the constraint that prevents Palettice Phase 2 from over-generalising — what is the test that Palettice's abstractions are not diverging from shadow-work's production needs?

The six expansion items are listed 'in rough dependency order' with items 1-3 described as migration-driven and items 4-6 as Culture-game-driven. But Open Question 4 (country-as-Soul) explicitly raises the possibility that aggregation Souls (item 4) are migration-critical if shadow-work's country is treated as a Soul. The brainstorm acknowledges this but leaves it unresolved ('worth answering early in the next planning step'). If aggregation Souls turn out to be migration-critical, the migration's scope expands from 'items 1-3' to 'items 1-4,' which is a significant scope change that should be resolved before the migration epic is opened, not discovered mid-sprint.

The Prometheus Crisis demo question (Open Question 5) has three sub-answers, all described as 'compatible with migration priority.' But the choice between pre-migration cut, post-migration ship, and demo-retired has concrete implications for the migration's scope and pace that the brainstorm does not trace through. Pre-migration cut requires shadow-work to maintain two stable branches (demo-branch and migration-branch) simultaneously. Post-migration ship requires the migration to be production-quality before any external validation of the gameplay loop. Demo-retired removes schedule pressure but creates motivation risk on the shadow-work side. The brainstorm calls this 'the user's call' but does not give the user the information needed to make an informed choice.

The migration plan has no rollback path. If Palettice Phase 2 turns out not to generalise shadow-work's production cases correctly (e.g., the archetype derivation is subtly wrong, the ±20 cap order differs, the stress feedback loop is missing), shadow-work needs to revert to its AgentPersonality implementation. A migration without a rollback path is a bet that the first Palettice Phase 2 implementation is correct. In a production system used for real gameplay calibration, this is a high-risk assumption. The brainstorm should either define a rollback path (shadow-work keeps AgentPersonality as a fallback behind a feature flag) or explicitly accept that rollback is not available and state what that implies for testing requirements.

severity_examples.condition: Without a defined 'migration complete' state, the migration is declared done whenever it is convenient to declare it done. In a project where demo schedule is already in tension with migration priority, the politically convenient stopping point is 'shadow-work compiles against Palettice' — which may not include evolution writes as SoulEvents, which may not include archetype derivation, which may not include stress. The work that remains gets re-labelled as Phase 2 and the debt accumulates.
severity_examples.scenario: Migration completion criterion absent — stalls at 70%

severity_examples.condition: If 80+ institutional agents become Souls (SoulId in shadow-work, personality state in Palettice), then every 'deployment causes institutional-agent personality shift' event is a cross-codebase write. This is a dual-write scenario: shadow-work writes the deployment event, and Palettice must receive a corresponding SoulEvent. If either write fails, the two systems are inconsistent. The migration plan needs to address this write path explicitly, including failure recovery.
severity_examples.scenario: Institutional agent personality writes cross codebase boundary on every event

severity_examples.condition: If Open Question 4 (country-as-Soul) resolves to 'yes, country is a Soul,' and this is discovered after the migration epic is opened with items 1-3 as scope, the sprint plan is invalidated mid-execution. The cost of scope discovery after planning is higher than the cost of resolving the question before planning.
severity_examples.scenario: Aggregation Soul scope discovered as migration-critical mid-sprint

success_hints: Check for a definition of 'migration complete' — if it is not present, flag this as the single highest-risk omission in the migration commitment

Trace the write path for 'a gameplay event causes personality change in an institutional agent' under the proposed migration architecture and verify it does not cross codebase boundaries in a way that introduces dual-write risk
Verify that Open Question 4 (country-as-Soul) is resolved or explicitly scoped out before the migration epic is opened — scope ambiguity at epic-open time is a predictable sprint-failure cause

Check whether there is a rollback path for shadow-work if Palettice Phase 2 produces incorrect archetype derivations or evolution behaviour — if not, flag what testing guarantees are required to make the no-rollback bet safe
task_context: The document makes a migration-as-priority commitment: shadow-work's personality system will be absorbed into Palettice Phase 2, with shadow-work refactoring to consume Palettice. This review focuses on whether the migration commitment is adequately specified — completion criterion, scope boundaries, cross-codebase write path, rollback strategy — and flags the process-level risks that are most likely to cause the migration to stall or produce inconsistency.
